pl-l2d22c5-d1e108.summary: States that some ignorance excuses the sinner and some does not, invincible and vincible; all excuse is removed where the command is known.
claims: Knowledge of the command removes excuse.

pl-l2d22c5-d1e113.summary: Distinguishes three kinds of ignorance: of those who will not know though able, which does not excuse, being itself sin; of those who wish but cannot, which excuses and is punishment of sin, not sin; and of those who simply do not know, neither refusing nor seeking, which does not fully excuse but perhaps lessens punishment.

pl-l2d22c5-d1e116.summary: Cites Augustine to Valentinus: those who know God's commands lose the excuse of ignorance; though sinning knowingly is graver, one may not flee to ignorance for excuse. Ignorance is sin in those who would not understand, punishment in those who could not; simple ignorance excuses no one from eternal fire, but perhaps so that he burns more mildly.
claims: Ignorance is sin in some, punishment in others.
Simple ignorance may lessen but not remove punishment.

pl-l2d22c5-d1e135.summary: Concludes that the woman had no excuse of ignorance, since she knew the command and that acting otherwise was sin.

pl-l2d22c5-d1e138.summary: Asks whence consent to evil came, since human nature was without vice.

pl-l2d22c5-d1e141.summary: Answers: from the free choice of the will. The cause of man's becoming worse was both in another, the devil who persuaded, and in himself, consenting by free will; since free choice is good, that evil consent came from a good thing. This will be treated more fully with the origin of evil.
claims: Evil consent came from free choice.
Evil arose from a good thing.

pl-l2d22c5.summary: Distinguishes ignorance that excuses and that which does not, invincible and vincible; no excuse remains where the command is known. Ignorance is threefold: of those who will not know though they could, which is itself sin; of those who would but cannot, which excuses and is punishment, not sin; and of those who simply do not know, which does not fully excuse but perhaps lessens punishment (Augustine to Valentinus). So the woman had no excuse. Asked whence consent to evil came when nature was without vice, Lombard answers: from free choice, the cause being both in the devil who persuaded and in man who consented; and since free choice is good, the evil consent came from a good thing, to be treated more fully later.
claims: Some ignorance excuses and some does not.
Where the command is known, there is no excuse.
Invincible ignorance excuses and is a punishment of sin.
Simple ignorance does not fully excuse but may lessen punishment.
The first evil consent came from free choice, a good thing.
The cause of man's becoming worse was both the devil's suggestion and man's consent.
